prompt: `ana:x:1001:1002::/home/ana:/bin/bash`. What is the `x` in the second field?
hint: It used to be something else, and it moved for a reason.

choices.text: A placeholder for an account that has no password set
choices.why: An account with no password shows an empty field there, which is a different thing.

choices.text: A flag marking the account as locked
choices.why: Locking puts an exclamation mark in front of the hash, in the other file.

choices.text: A pointer saying the hash is in /etc/shadow
choices.why: Right, and it moved because this file has to stay readable by everybody.

choices.text: The first character of a truncated password hash
choices.why: No part of a hash is kept here; the field holds one character and it is always the same one.

prompt: Why is `/etc/passwd` mode 644 while `/etc/shadow` is 640?
hint: One of them is needed by a command you run constantly.

choices.text: `ls -l` has to turn a UID into a name
choices.why: Right — the split exists so the mapping stays public and the secret does not.

choices.text: `/etc/shadow` changes more often, so it is protected against corruption
choices.why: Permissions decide who reads it, and they say nothing about how often it changes.

choices.text: `/etc/passwd` is a cache of `/etc/shadow`, with the sensitive half left out
choices.why: Neither is a cache of the other; they hold different fields about the same accounts.

choices.text: The group `shadow` owns both, and 644 is what the package happened to ship
choices.why: The modes are deliberate, and `ls -l` shows a different group on each.

prompt: An account's shell is `/usr/sbin/nologin`. What can it still do?
hint: It was created for something, and that something is not typing.

choices.text: It is disabled, so files and services are out of reach for it
choices.why: It owns files and runs services; what it lacks is a way in.

choices.text: It logs in, and the shell exits after printing a warning
choices.why: The program refuses rather than leaving a usable session behind.

choices.text: It logs in over ssh but has no shell for a console session
choices.why: The refusal applies to both; ssh gets the same program.

choices.text: Own files and run services
choices.why: Right — that is what the twenty-nine non-people accounts in section 71 are for.

prompt: Why prefer `getent passwd ana` over `grep '^ana:' /etc/passwd`?
hint: Think about a machine whose accounts come from somewhere else.

choices.text: `getent` reads the file faster on a large machine
choices.why: Speed is beside the point; on a small machine they take the same time.

choices.text: `getent` asks the name service, so it finds accounts from a directory too
choices.why: Right — LDAP or Active Directory accounts are absent from the file and present in the system.

choices.text: `grep` needs a regular expression and `getent` takes a plain name
choices.why: Both take what you type; what differs is where they look.

choices.text: `getent` requires root while `grep` works for anybody, so it is more trustworthy
choices.why: Both work for an ordinary user, and neither reads the shadow file.

prompt: Below which UID does a distribution reserve the numbers for system accounts rather than people?
hint: A round number.

prompt: A colleague says the support team can look up a forgotten password. What is wrong with that?
hint: Look at what the second field of a shadow line actually holds.

choices.text: Support lacks the group membership to read the file
choices.why: Membership decides who reads it, and reading it would still not yield a password.

choices.text: The field is encrypted, and support has no key
choices.why: There is no key. It is a hash, and hashing runs one way.

choices.text: The password is there, and printing it would be against policy
choices.why: It is not there at all, which is a stronger fact than a policy.

choices.text: What is stored is a hash, which cannot be run backwards
choices.why: Right, and that is why resetting is normal and retrieving is a red flag.

prompt: Two accounts choose the same password. Why do their stored hashes differ?
hint: Something random is stored in the clear beside each hash.

choices.text: The hash includes the account name, so it differs per user
choices.why: The name is not part of the input; a random value is.

choices.text: Each account gets its own random salt
choices.why: Right, so a precomputed table would have to be rebuilt for each one.

choices.text: The algorithm seeds itself from the time the password was set
choices.why: The time is in a later field, and it is not an input to the hash.

choices.text: They are hashed with different algorithms chosen at account creation
choices.why: The algorithm is a system setting and is normally the same for both.

prompt: You hand somebody a new account with a temporary password. What makes them change it at first login?
hint: One field says when it was last changed, and setting it to zero is the trick.

choices.text: passwd -e newuser
choices.why: That is not a flag passwd has; the ageing tool is the one with it.

choices.text: usermod -L newuser
choices.why: That locks the account, which is the opposite of letting them in.

choices.text: chage -d 0 newuser
choices.why: Right: last changed becomes the epoch, so it is overdue immediately.

choices.text: chage -M 0 newuser
choices.why: A maximum age of zero is a different and stranger setting.

prompt: Somebody leaves. You run `passwd -l` on their account and they still log in. How?
hint: One authentication path never touches that file.

choices.text: An ssh key in their authorized_keys
choices.why: Right — keys never consult the shadow file, which is why the two steps go together.

choices.text: The lock takes effect at the next reboot, and not before
choices.why: It is written immediately; the login used a different path.

choices.text: `passwd -l` locks the password and leaves the account usable by sudo
choices.why: sudo asks for a password too, so a lock would stop it.

choices.text: Their session was open before the lock, and it survived
choices.why: A surviving session would explain one connection, and they logged in afresh.

prompt: Which command prints an account's password ageing settings as readable dates?
hint: Two words, and the first is five letters.

prompt: `useradd dora` succeeds and `ls -ld /home/dora` says no such directory. Is something broken?
hint: The command did exactly what it was asked and nothing more.

choices.text: Yes — the account is unusable until the directory is created by hand
choices.why: It logs in and lands in / with an error, which is bad and is not the same as unusable.

choices.text: Yes — useradd should have failed rather than record a path it did not create
choices.why: It records the path it was told to record, and creating it is a separate flag.

choices.text: No — `-m` is what creates it, and it was left out
choices.why: Right, and `adduser` is the friendlier front end that assumes you meant `-m`.

choices.text: No — the directory appears at the account's first login
choices.why: Nothing creates it later; the login just fails to find it.

prompt: After `userdel dorasilva`, `ls -ld /home/dora` prints `1005` where a name used to be. What happened?
hint: Nothing about the files changed.

choices.text: The directory was reassigned to the next free account
choices.why: Reassignment would print that account's name; there is nothing to print.

choices.text: The line that mapped 1005 to a name is gone
choices.why: Right — the filesystem stored the number all along, as lesson 4 section 60 said.

choices.text: `userdel` rewrote the ownership to a reserved value
choices.why: It touched no files; the owner field is what it always was.

choices.text: The directory lost its group, so `ls` falls back to numbers for both columns
choices.why: The group column still prints a name, which rules that out.

prompt: Why is deleting an account before dealing with its files a problem on a small machine?
hint: Think about what the next account created will be given.

choices.text: The files become unreadable once the name is gone
choices.why: They keep their mode; a number owns them and the mode still applies.

choices.text: `userdel` refuses to run while the account owns files elsewhere
choices.why: It runs, and it says nothing about files outside the home directory.

choices.text: Orphaned files are removed by a nightly job
choices.why: No such job exists; they sit there indefinitely.

choices.text: The next account gets the freed UID and inherits them
choices.why: Right, so somebody who arrives owns files belonging to somebody who left.

prompt: What is `/etc/skel` for?
hint: It explains three files that appeared in a brand-new home directory.

choices.text: It is copied into a new home directory by `useradd -m`
choices.why: Right, and it is how a company default reaches every account made afterwards.

choices.text: It holds the default settings the shell falls back on when a home is missing
choices.why: The shell falls back on the system-wide files in /etc, and this is not one of them.

choices.text: It is where `userdel` archives a deleted account's files
choices.why: Nothing archives them; `-r` deletes and the default leaves them alone.

choices.text: It is a template reapplied to each account whenever the system starts
choices.why: It is copied once, at creation, and existing accounts are never revisited.

prompt: Write the `useradd` line that creates `dora` with a home directory and bash as her shell.
hint: Two flags, and one of them takes a path.

prompt: `who` prints nothing on a machine where several shells are running. What does that mean?
hint: Those commands read a file that something has to write.

choices.text: The shells belong to system accounts, which who leaves out
choices.why: It lists any account with a session; the accounts are not the filter.

choices.text: who reads the process table and found no shell marked as a login
choices.why: It never reads the process table; it reads a record file.

choices.text: The sessions are older than the file's retention window
choices.why: Current sessions are in utmp regardless of age.

choices.text: Nothing wrote a session record — no login or sshd was involved
choices.why: Right, and it is the normal state of a container.

prompt: A PATH set in `~/.bashrc` works when you log in and is missing in `ssh host 'somecommand'`. Why?
hint: That third form starts a shell of a kind that reads neither file.

choices.text: ssh strips the environment before running a remote command
choices.why: It carries little across, and the remote shell's own startup is what differs here.

choices.text: `~/.bashrc` is read by login shells alone, and that is not one
choices.why: It is the other way round: bashrc is for interactive shells.

choices.text: The remote shell is non-interactive
choices.why: Right — and it is why an environment belongs where a child process inherits it.

choices.text: The command runs before the home directory is mounted
choices.why: The home is there; nothing about mounting is involved.

prompt: Which belongs in `~/.profile` rather than in `~/.bashrc`?
hint: One of the two is inherited by child processes.

choices.text: export EDITOR=vim
choices.why: Right — environment, and every child gets it.

choices.text: alias ll='ls -la'
choices.why: An alias is a shell convenience and is not inherited at all.
The prompt is only meaningful in an interactive shell.

choices.text: shopt -s histappend
choices.why: A shell option, and it belongs with the other interactive settings.

prompt: `tty` answers `not a tty`. What is that telling you?
hint: A program uses this to decide whether somebody is watching.

choices.text: The terminal emulator is misconfigured
choices.why: Nothing is wrong; the shell's input is simply not a terminal.

choices.text: The shell's input is a pipe or a script
choices.why: Right, and programs read it to decide about colour, prompts and progress bars.

choices.text: You are connected over ssh rather than sitting at the machine
choices.why: An ssh session gets a pty, and `tty` prints its name.

choices.text: Your account has no login shell recorded in /etc/passwd
choices.why: Field 7 has nothing to do with it; the shell is running and answering.

prompt: The first connection to a host asks you to confirm a fingerprint. What is it a fingerprint of?
hint: The other end has an identity too.

choices.text: Your own public key, so the server knows which to expect
choices.why: Your key goes in authorized_keys; nothing hashes it at you.

choices.text: The connection, so a later session can be matched to this one
choices.why: Sessions are not tracked that way, and the value is stable across connections.

choices.text: The server's own host key
choices.why: Right, and accepting it writes the key into your known_hosts.

choices.text: The account's password hash, sent so the client can verify it offline
choices.why: A password hash never leaves the server, and this happens before any password.

prompt: Which of the two files `ssh-keygen` made is safe to paste into a chat message?
hint: One of them has a suffix.

choices.text: id_ed25519.pub
choices.why: Right — the public half is meant to be copied around.

choices.text: id_ed25519
choices.why: That is the private key, and pasting it hands over the account.

choices.text: Either — the pair is useless without both
choices.why: The private half alone is enough to log in.

choices.text: Neither — both halves have to stay on the machine that made them
choices.why: The public half exists precisely to be given away.

prompt: What is the difference between `authorized_keys` and `known_hosts`?
hint: One is about people coming in, the other about machines you went out to.

choices.text: One holds private keys and the other holds public ones
choices.why: Both hold public keys; what differs is whose.

choices.text: Keys allowed in, against servers you accepted
choices.why: Right, and they answer opposite questions from the same directory.

choices.text: The first is written by ssh and the second by ssh-keygen
choices.why: Both are written by ssh or its helpers; authorship is not the distinction.

choices.text: The first applies to this machine and the second to the whole network
choices.why: Both are yours alone, in your own home directory.

prompt: You get the REMOTE HOST IDENTIFICATION HAS CHANGED banner. What is the right first move?
hint: Three things cause it and they are not equally innocent.

choices.text: Run `ssh-keygen -R host` so the connection goes through
choices.why: That is the fix for the innocent case, and running it first skips deciding which case it is.

choices.text: Add StrictHostKeyChecking=no to stop it happening again
choices.why: That removes the check entirely, which is the protection the banner exists to give you.

choices.text: Connect with a password instead, which does not use host keys
choices.why: Host keys are checked before any authentication method is chosen.

choices.text: Find out whether the server was rebuilt
choices.why: Right — rebuilt, a different machine behind the name, or interception, in that order.

prompt: Which command copies your public key into another account's `authorized_keys` for you?
hint: Three words joined by hyphens.

prompt: A program keeps running after you log out, without you taking any special step. What is it?
hint: Three kinds of long-running process, and one of them belongs to the system.

choices.text: A background job, detached from your shell
choices.why: That one ends with your session unless you take a step, which is the stated condition.

choices.text: A service, started by the init system
choices.why: Right — it belongs to the machine rather than to your session.

choices.text: A scheduled job, waiting for its next time
choices.why: A scheduled job is not running between firings; it is started fresh each time.

choices.text: A zombie, left behind because its parent stopped collecting it
choices.why: A zombie holds a table entry and runs nothing at all.

prompt: Why does a web server run as `www-data` rather than as root?
hint: Ask what an attacker gets when that program is broken into.

choices.text: Root is reserved for interactive logins and services use other accounts
choices.why: Plenty of services do run as root; the reason is about consequence rather than reservation.

choices.text: Binding a network port requires a non-root account on modern Linux
choices.why: Low ports historically needed root, which runs the other way.

choices.text: A break-in then yields that account, and no more
choices.why: Right — one account per service is the cheapest boundary the system has.

choices.text: Files written by root would be unreadable to the service later
choices.why: root's files are readable by root; ownership is not the constraint here.

prompt: A service's working data is on disk. Which directory should it be in?
hint: Lesson 3 section 37 divides these by what changes.

choices.text: /var/lib/<name>
choices.why: Right — data the machine writes while running.

choices.text: /etc/<name>
choices.why: Configuration lives there, and it is read rather than written.

choices.text: /usr/lib/<name>
choices.why: Installed files, owned by the package manager.

choices.text: /opt/<name>
choices.why: A vendor's tree for software outside the package manager.

prompt: Why does a program written for systemd stay in the foreground instead of daemonising?
hint: Something else is now doing the detaching.

choices.text: Foreground processes are given a higher scheduling priority
choices.why: Priority is set separately, and it has nothing to do with detaching.

choices.text: systemd refuses to start a process that forks
choices.why: Type=forking exists precisely for programs that do.

choices.text: A process that detached would be unable to write to the journal
choices.why: It can, through the ordinary streams; collection is not what changed.

choices.text: systemd does the detaching and tracking itself
choices.why: Right — and a program that forks anyway has to be declared with Type=forking.

prompt: How many programs does the kernel start directly at boot?
hint: Everything else descends from it.

choices.text: One per target listed in the default target
choices.why: Targets are units systemd reaches; the kernel knows about none of them.

choices.text: One per CPU, which then share out the work
choices.why: Processor count decides nothing about how many programs are started.

choices.text: One
choices.why: Right — process 1, and every other process is a descendant of it.

choices.text: Two: an init system and a logger, so early failures are recorded
choices.why: The logger is started by the init system like everything else.

prompt: `S20nginx` in `/etc/rc3.d` is a SysV startup link. What does the number do?
hint: The scripts were run in one order, and something had to decide it.

choices.text: It is the runlevel the script belongs to
choices.why: The runlevel is the `3` in the directory name.

choices.text: It is the number of seconds to wait before starting
choices.why: Nothing waits; the scripts run one after another.

choices.text: It is the exit status the script should return on success
choices.why: Zero is success there as everywhere.

choices.text: It sets the position in the alphabetical order
choices.why: Right, and that ordering was a guess at dependencies rather than a statement of them.

prompt: Which systemd idea made `systemctl stop` reliable where SysV's stop script was not?
hint: It is about knowing what you started.

choices.text: Each service's processes are tracked in a cgroup
choices.why: Right — the kernel keeps the list, so processes that forked away are stopped too.

choices.text: Units are declarative, so the stop path is generated rather than written
choices.why: Declarative units are a real improvement and they do not track a running process.

choices.text: Services start in parallel, so stopping happens in reverse order
choices.why: Reverse ordering is real and says nothing about which processes are found.

choices.text: The journal records each PID a service has had
choices.why: The journal records what was said, and stopping does not read it.

prompt: What does `docker run --init` add, and why would a container need it?
hint: Two jobs belong to process one, and an application program does neither.

choices.text: A shell, so the container has somewhere to run startup commands
choices.why: A shell runs commands and does not adopt or reap anything.

choices.text: A tiny process one that adopts orphans and reaps them
choices.why: Right, and without it a container leaks zombies until its table fills.

choices.text: A logging collector, so the container's output reaches the host
choices.why: Output already reaches the host through the ordinary streams.

choices.text: A supervisor that restarts the main program when it exits
choices.why: Restart policy is a separate flag and a separate idea.

prompt: You set a service up, checked it was running, rebooted, and it is gone. What was missed?
hint: Two verbs, two moments.

choices.text: `daemon-reload`, so systemd had yet to read the unit
choices.why: It read the unit; the service ran before the reboot.

choices.text: `unmask`, since a masked service is refused a start
choices.why: A masked service would have refused to start in the first place.

choices.text: `systemctl restart`, which makes the state permanent
choices.why: Restarting is another now-verb and changes nothing about the next boot.

choices.text: `systemctl enable`
choices.why: Right — `start` is now, `enable` is at the next boot.

prompt: `systemctl enable` printed `Created symlink …/multi-user.target.wants/hello.service`. What did it do?
hint: Read the path it made.

choices.text: Added the unit to a list a target reads at boot
choices.why: Right, and a symlink starts nothing, which is the whole of why enable is not start.

choices.text: Copied the unit into the directory systemd loads from
choices.why: It linked rather than copied, and the original stays where it was.

choices.text: Registered the service with the journal so its output is kept
choices.why: Output is collected whether or not a service is enabled.

choices.text: Started the service and recorded that it should start again
choices.why: Nothing was started; `--now` is the flag that would have.

prompt: A web server is serving traffic and its configuration changed. `restart` or `reload`?
hint: One of the two drops what is connected.

choices.text: restart, because a reload leaves the old configuration in memory
choices.why: A reload is exactly a re-read of the configuration.

choices.text: restart, because reload is a Debian extension and is missing elsewhere
choices.why: It is standard, and whether a service supports it is in its own unit file.

choices.text: reload
choices.why: Right — it re-reads without dropping connections, and nginx supports it.

choices.text: Either — systemd treats them as the same verb for network services
choices.why: They are separate verbs that run separate commands from the unit.

prompt: `systemctl is-enabled foo` says `static`. What does that mean?
hint: Enabling writes a symlink somewhere, and something has to say where.

choices.text: The unit is compiled into systemd rather than read from a file
choices.why: Every unit is a file; nothing is compiled in.

choices.text: The unit has no [Install] section
choices.why: Right — something else pulls it in, and enabling it would have no meaning.

choices.text: The unit is linked to /dev/null, so a start is refused
choices.why: That is `masked`, and it is a different answer from the same command.

choices.text: The unit was enabled by the package and is yours to leave alone
choices.why: A packaged unit is disabled like any other; the file decides, not the packager.

prompt: Write the command that starts a service now and also arranges for it at the next boot, in one go, for `nginx`.
hint: One verb and one flag.

prompt: `Active: active (exited)` on a unit. Did it fail?
hint: Some units have nothing left running when they succeed.

choices.text: Yes — `exited` is how a crash is reported
choices.why: A crash reports `failed`, and this word is on the active side of the line.

choices.text: No — it ran, finished, and that was the job
choices.why: Right, and a unit that mounts something or sets a value looks exactly like this.

choices.text: Yes — the process left, so the service is no longer being watched
choices.why: Nothing is being watched, and that is the intended end state.

choices.text: It depends on whether the unit has a Restart policy set
choices.why: The restart policy decides what happens after a failure, and this is not one.

prompt: `Loaded: loaded (…; disabled)` on a service that is currently running. What does that tell you?
hint: Two words on the same line, about two different moments.

choices.text: The unit file was edited after the service started
choices.why: Editing is not recorded on that line; a stale unit shows nothing here.

choices.text: The service is running from a drop-in rather than the main unit
choices.why: Drop-ins are shown by `systemctl cat`, and they do not change this word.

choices.text: systemd lost track of it, so the enabled state is unreadable
choices.why: It read a definite answer, and that answer is `disabled`.

choices.text: Somebody started it by hand
choices.why: Right, and that is the pair of facts the line exists to show together.

prompt: A service's status is red. Which line do you read first?
hint: One possible answer makes the other three irrelevant.

choices.text: `Loaded:` — if the unit is `not-found`, nothing else matters
choices.why: Right: a missing or misnamed unit file makes every other line noise.

choices.text: The journal lines at the bottom, since the program says most
choices.why: They usually hold the answer, and they are worth nothing if there is no unit.

choices.text: `Main PID:`, to find the process and look at it directly
choices.why: A failed service has no process left to look at.

choices.text: `Active:`, because the Result word names the kind of failure
choices.why: That is the second line to read, and the first one can rule it out.

prompt: What does the `CGroup:` tree in a status block list?
hint: It is section 77's third idea, made visible.

choices.text: The units this service depends on
choices.why: Dependencies are in the unit file and are shown elsewhere.

choices.text: The threads inside the main process
choices.why: Threads are counted in Tasks; these lines have their own PIDs.

choices.text: Each process the service owns
choices.why: Right, and it is what makes `systemctl stop` reliable.

choices.text: The processes that have the service's files open
choices.why: That is what lsof answers, and it would list other accounts' processes too.

prompt: `ExecStart=/usr/bin/foo > /var/log/foo.log` in a unit file. What happens?
hint: There is no shell reading that line.

choices.text: The output is redirected, as it would be in a shell
choices.why: A shell would do that, and systemd is not running one.

choices.text: systemd refuses to load the unit and reports a syntax error
choices.why: It loads happily; the line is valid and means something else.

choices.text: The redirect is applied and the journal is left empty
choices.why: The journal receives the output, because the redirect never happened.

choices.text: `foo` is started with `>` and the path as two arguments
choices.why: Right — and `ExecStart=/bin/sh -c '…'` is how you ask for a shell on purpose.

prompt: You need one line changed in a packaged unit. Why `systemctl edit` rather than copying the file to `/etc`?
hint: Ask what happens at the next package upgrade.

choices.text: A drop-in inherits the rest, and keeps upgrading
choices.why: Right — a full copy in /etc wins forever and silently stops improving.

choices.text: A copy in /etc has lower priority and would be ignored
choices.why: It has higher priority, which is exactly why it wins and why that is the trap.

choices.text: `systemctl edit` writes the change into the package's own file
choices.why: It never touches the packaged file; that is the point of a drop-in.

choices.text: A copy in /etc has to be registered before systemd will read it
choices.why: It is read because of where it sits, with nothing to register.

prompt: `systemd-analyze verify` says `Unknown key name 'Descriptoin' in section 'Unit', ignoring.` Why is that dangerous?
hint: Read the last word.

choices.text: It means the whole unit was rejected and the service stays down
choices.why: The unit loaded; one line was dropped.

choices.text: It means the key was applied with a default value
choices.why: Nothing was applied; the line was discarded.

choices.text: The line was dropped and the service starts with no complaint
choices.why: Right — a typo in a key name is silence, not an error, which is why verify exists.

choices.text: It means the section header is wrong and the keys below it are lost
choices.why: One key is named, and the section it names is a real one.

prompt: Which `Type=` is right for a program that stays in the foreground?
hint: The other one is for a program that forks and lets the parent exit.

choices.text: forking
choices.why: That is for a program that daemonises itself, and it makes this one hang.

choices.text: simple
choices.why: Right, and it is the default because it is the common case.

choices.text: oneshot
choices.why: That is for something that runs and finishes on purpose.

choices.text: notify
choices.why: That is for a program written to tell systemd when it is ready.

prompt: Which command checks a unit file for mistakes without starting anything?
hint: Two words, and the first is hyphenated.

prompt: Where does a systemd service's printed output go?
hint: Section 76 said a daemon has no terminal.

choices.text: To the terminal that ran `systemctl start`
choices.why: That terminal is gone the moment the command returns.

choices.text: To a file named after the unit in /var/log
choices.why: Some services write there themselves; systemd does not put it there.

choices.text: To the journal, which collects it
choices.why: Right, and it is why a unit should print rather than manage a log file.

choices.text: Nowhere, unless the unit sets StandardOutput explicitly
choices.why: The default already sends it to the journal.

prompt: `journalctl -u nginx` prints nothing when you run it as an ordinary user. What is the likely reason?
hint: Two groups grant the access.

choices.text: You are in neither `systemd-journal` nor `adm`
choices.why: Right — try it with sudo before concluding the service said nothing.

choices.text: nginx writes to /var/log rather than to the journal
choices.why: Worth checking, and an empty result for one user and not another points elsewhere.

choices.text: The journal was vacuumed and the entries are gone
choices.why: Vacuuming removes old entries for everybody, not for one account.

choices.text: `-u` matches the unit name exactly and yours is nginx.service
choices.why: The suffix is assumed, and it would fail the same way for root.

prompt: A machine's journal is empty after every reboot. What is missing?
hint: It has two possible homes, and one of them is in memory.

choices.text: A Storage= setting in the unit files of each service
choices.why: Storage is a journald setting, and it is not per service.

choices.text: The `adm` group, without which old entries are hidden
choices.why: Group membership decides who reads, not how long entries survive.

choices.text: A vacuum policy, which is keeping the journal at zero size
choices.why: Vacuuming prunes old entries and leaves recent ones.

choices.text: The directory /var/log/journal
choices.why: Right — without it the journal lives on a tmpfs and goes at boot.

prompt: A service failed because something it depends on failed first. `journalctl -u thatservice` shows only its own confusion. What next?
hint: One flag shows the machine rather than the unit.

choices.text: journalctl -u thatservice -n 200, for more of the same
choices.why: More lines of one unit is more of the same confusion.

choices.text: journalctl -b, which shows the boot in order
choices.why: Right — the first failure is above the second, and the cascade becomes readable.

choices.text: systemctl status thatservice, for the fields the journal lacks
choices.why: Its status block prints the same ten lines you already read.

choices.text: journalctl --disk-usage, to rule out a truncated journal
choices.why: Worth a glance, and truncation would have removed old entries rather than the cause.

prompt: Write the journalctl that follows one service's log as it is written, for `nginx`.
hint: Two flags, and the second is one letter.

prompt: What is a target?
hint: It has no ExecStart.

choices.text: A service that starts other services in sequence
choices.why: It runs no program at all, which a service does.

choices.text: A named group of units
choices.why: Right — a name for a state, and enabling puts a service in its wants directory.

choices.text: A runlevel number rewritten as a word
choices.why: Several targets have no runlevel equivalent, and targets compose.

choices.text: The unit systemd loads first when the kernel hands over control
choices.why: The first unit is the default target, and that is one target among many.

prompt: A unit has `After=network.target` and still fails at boot while working by hand. Why?
hint: That target is reached earlier than people assume.

choices.text: `After=` means before, and the two are the wrong way round
choices.why: It means after, and the order is what it says.

choices.text: The unit needs Requires= as well, or After= is ignored
choices.why: After= applies on its own; ordering and dependency are separate.

choices.text: That target means configured rather than reachable
choices.why: Right — `network-online.target`, with a Wants=, is the honest version.

choices.text: Targets are honoured just for services started by hand
choices.why: They are how boot order is decided in the first place.

prompt: A boot drops you at `Give root password for maintenance`. What is the most likely cause?
hint: Lesson 3 section 47 gave you the rehearsal for this.

choices.text: A filesystem in /etc/fstab could not be mounted
choices.why: Right, and `sudo mount -a` before rebooting is the rehearsal that avoids it.

choices.text: The default target was set to rescue by mistake
choices.why: That would give you a rescue shell without asking about a filesystem.

choices.text: A service with Restart=on-failure is failing in a loop
choices.why: A looping service does not stop the boot; it fails in the background.

choices.text: The root account has no password, so login is refused
choices.why: That is why the prompt may be unanswerable, and it is not what caused it.

prompt: Two systemd-analyze subcommands: one sorts units by duration, the other follows what the total was waiting on. Which answers 'why did the boot take so long'?
hint: One lists what was slow; the other lists what was waited on.

choices.text: blame, because it sorts by duration
choices.why: It sorts by duration, and a slow unit nobody waited for cost nothing.

choices.text: Either — they print the same units in a different order
choices.why: They select differently, not merely order differently.

choices.text: blame, once you subtract the units that ran in parallel
choices.why: There is no such subtraction to do by hand.

choices.text: critical-chain
choices.why: Right — it shows the chain the total was actually waiting on.

prompt: Which systemctl subcommand prints the units systemd is currently waiting on, for a boot that has hung?
hint: Two words, and the second is a plural noun.

prompt: You arrive at a machine somebody says is broken. Which command do you run first?
hint: One of these prints a short list and it is usually the answer.

choices.text: journalctl -b
choices.why: A whole boot of log, before you know what you are looking for.

choices.text: systemctl list-units --type=service
choices.why: Several hundred lines, most of them healthy.

choices.text: systemctl --failed
choices.why: Right — the services that tried and did not make it, usually one line.

choices.text: systemctl status
choices.why: Without a unit name that prints the machine's overall state, which is vaguer.

prompt: Which field of `/etc/passwd` decides whether an account can get a shell? Give its number.
hint: Count the colons; it is the last field.

prompt: A service is `active (running)` and `Loaded: … disabled`. What happens at the next reboot?
hint: Two words, two moments.

choices.text: It does not come back
choices.why: Right, and nothing warns you until the reboot happens.

choices.text: It comes back, because it was running when the machine went down
choices.why: Nothing records what was running; the enabled state is what decides.

choices.text: It comes back in a degraded state and logs a warning
choices.why: There is no such halfway state; it either starts or does not.

choices.text: It comes back, because `disabled` refers to the unit file rather than to boot
choices.why: The word refers to exactly the boot question.

prompt: Somebody leaves the company. You lock their password. What else has to happen before the account is really shut?
hint: One authentication path never reads the password file.

choices.text: Their primary group has to be changed
choices.why: Group membership decides file access, and it lets nobody log in.

choices.text: Their home directory has to be removed
choices.why: Removing it costs you their files and stops no login.

choices.text: Their shell has to be set to nologin
choices.why: A good step, and a key-based session can still be refused elsewhere first.

choices.text: Their authorized_keys has to go
choices.why: Right — keys never consult the shadow file, which is section 75's warning.

prompt: Write the command that shows a unit file together with every drop-in applied on top of it, for `nginx`.
hint: Two words and a name.

prompt: You edit `/etc/systemd/system/foo.service` by hand and restart the service. The change has no effect. What was missed?
hint: systemd read the unit once, at boot.

choices.text: `systemctl enable`, which rereads the file
choices.why: Enabling writes a symlink and rereads nothing.

choices.text: `systemctl daemon-reload`
choices.why: Right, and `systemctl edit` does it for you, which is one reason to prefer it.

choices.text: `systemd-analyze verify`, which loads the new version
choices.why: It checks a file and changes nothing in the running systemd.

choices.text: A reboot, since unit files are read at boot alone
choices.why: A reload is enough, and a reboot would work for the same reason.

prompt: Put these in the order you would work through a service that is not running.
trap: Narrow to the service, read what systemd thinks, then what the program said, then the machine.

prompt: Match each command to the moment it acts on.
hint: Two are about now and two are about the next boot.

pairs.right: now, and gone after a reboot
the next boot, and nothing right now
which state the machine boots into

right_distractors: stops everything not in the named target
checks a unit file without starting it

prompt: An account is created with `useradd -r` instead of plainly. What differs?
hint: One flag decides which side of a number line the UID falls on.

choices.text: It is given a random password instead of an empty field
choices.why: Neither form sets a password; that is passwd's job.

choices.text: It is created without a group of its own
choices.why: A group is made either way unless you say otherwise.

choices.text: It gets a UID below 1000 and no home directory
choices.why: Right — a system account, which is what section 71's twenty-nine are.

choices.text: It is created locked, so nobody can use it until it is unlocked
choices.why: It has no password set, which stops a password login without being a lock.

prompt: Which file lists who may log in as you on this machine, without typing a password?
hint: It is in your own `.ssh` directory.

choices.text: ~/.ssh/authorized_keys
choices.why: Right — one key per line, and ssh-copy-id appends to it.

choices.text: ~/.ssh/known_hosts
choices.why: That holds server keys you accepted, which is the opposite direction.

choices.text: ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub
choices.why: That is your own public key, which goes into the first file on another machine.

choices.text: /etc/ssh/ssh_host_ed25519_key.pub
choices.why: That is this machine's identity to other people's clients.

prompt: A nightly job writes to a directory and the files come out with the wrong permissions. Your `~/.bashrc` sets a umask. Why does it not apply?
hint: Lesson 4 section 62 said where a service's umask lives.

choices.text: The job runs as a different account, so your dotfile is irrelevant
choices.why: True and not the mechanism: even as you, a scheduled job reads neither dotfile.

choices.text: The job is started by a scheduler, not by a shell of yours
choices.why: Right, and a unit's `UMask=` is where it belongs.

choices.text: A umask in a dotfile applies at login and expires with the session
choices.why: It applies to that shell and its children, and it does not expire.

choices.text: The directory's setgid bit overrides the umask for new files
choices.why: setgid decides the group and the umask still decides the bits.

prompt: Write the journalctl that shows only errors and worse from the current boot.
hint: Two flags, and one takes a three-letter value.

prompt: `systemctl isolate multi-user.target` on a running server. What is the risk?
hint: The verb is not start.

choices.text: It reboots the machine into that target
choices.why: Nothing reboots; the change is immediate and in place.

choices.text: It changes what the machine boots into from now on
choices.why: That is set-default, and it changes nothing right now.

choices.text: It refuses unless the target is already active
choices.why: It runs, which is the problem.

choices.text: It stops everything not in that target
choices.why: Right — useful in a rescue console, alarming over ssh.

prompt: What does the `d` at the end of `sshd`, `crond` and `systemd` stand for?
hint: It is the older word for a service.

choices.text: daily, from the scheduled jobs these programs grew out of
choices.why: None of the three is scheduled; they run continuously.

choices.text: distributed, from the era when they ran across several machines
choices.why: They run on one machine, like any other program.

choices.text: daemon
choices.why: Right, and it is the Unix word for a program with no terminal.

choices.text: driver, since they sit between programs and the kernel
choices.why: Drivers are kernel code; these are ordinary programs.
